data.text/markdown:
Can we rebuild Regrid's and Mireye's layers from public sources?

The question. Commercial parcel platforms sell many layers on top of the parcel map: owners, values, sales, zoning, buildings, addresses, flood zones and more. How many of those layers could an open rebuild cover from sources anyone can reach? Which are genuinely proprietary? And where is an advertised layer thinner or older than the marketing says? The two vendors.
  • Regrid sells US parcel data (160 million parcels) with add-ons for buildings, addresses, zoning and ownership.
  • Mireye is a Y Combinator (Summer 2026) start-up selling "physical world context for AI agents". It is one API and an MCP server that answers questions about a place with cited fields. It launched on Hacker News on 2026-09-03. Its field catalog is public JSON, so we can rate every field it sells.
The method.
  1. List every layer each vendor advertises, from its public docs.
  2. Rate each layer public and easy (one national or statewide source), public but scattered (public record, but it takes county-by-county work) or proprietary (licensed, bought or derived by the vendor).
  3. Read Regrid's own published coverage report to see where its layers are thin or stale.
  4. Count what public sources hold in three counties of different kinds, against what Regrid says it has there.
Everything is read from public pages and public endpoints at run time. We used no logins, vendor accounts or paid services. We record no owner names: owner fields are only counted.

1. What Regrid advertises

inventory/regrid_layers.csv lists the 40 layers and field groups Regrid documents on support.regrid.com. Each row has a short quote from the doc page, the rating and the public source that would replace it. The rating is our judgement; the why column gives the reason. Regrid publishes a coverage report with the share of parcels that have each field filled, county by county. Its first row is the nationwide fill rate. We download it and put that rate next to each layer.

data.text/html: 40 Regrid layers: 12 public and easy, 17 public but scattered, 11 proprietary

data.text/markdown:
2. What Mireye advertises

Mireye's catalog is machine-readable without a key: GET /v1/meta/fields lists the free point-lookup ("Fetch") fields and GET /v1/enrich/fields lists everything its paid parcel "Enrich" call returns. Each field names its source with a label such as FEMA_NFHL or USDA_SSURGO. We rate each of those source labels once, in inventory/mireye_sources.csv, and count fields.

data.text/html: 538 Mireye fields (351 Fetch, 187 Enrich-only) from 99 source labels:

data.text/markdown: Mireye never names its parcel vendor: the parcel fields are labelled PARCEL_VENDOR, and its terms forbid using them to "reconstruct a substantial portion of an underlying licensed dataset". The field names give it away. We compare them with the column names in Regrid's coverage report, where Mireye's pvd_ prefix ("parcel vendor data") stands for Regrid's own ll_.

161 of 165 Mireye PARCEL_VENDOR fields have a column of the same name in Regrid's coverage report. Not matched: geometry, parcel_match_distance_m, parcel_match_radius_m, parcel_match_type. The rest of Mireye's catalog is federal and open data: its parcel layer is Regrid's, resold.
Mireye's own field descriptions say where a field is narrower than "any US location". We count the fields whose description admits a limit.

data.text/markdown:
3. Regrid's coverage report against Regrid's claims

The coverage report gives every county's last refresh date and fill rates. We check them against three claims from Regrid's docs:
  • "We target updating over 3,000 counties (92%) on an at least annual basis" (data dictionary);
  • "On average 94% of our parcels have been refreshed in the last 12 months" (onboarding FAQ);
  • "100% US coverage" of parcels (parcel schemas).
Ages are measured from the day this notebook runs. To test "100%", we compare each county's parcel count with its 2020 Census housing units (from TIGERweb). Cities with large apartment buildings have far more homes than parcels, so we only flag counties under 100,000 housing units with fewer than half as many parcels.

Connecticut's 8 old counties are expected: Regrid uses its 9 new planning regions instead. The 60xxx and 69xxx codes are American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands.

data.text/markdown:
Most of these differences are stale pages, not overclaims: the report is newer and bigger than the marketing. The address pages disagree with each other by more than 100 million. That is a ready-to-use problem for a buyer, not a coverage problem.

4. Three counties

Three kinds of county:
  • Wake County, NC is urban, and both the county and the state (NC OneMap) publish parcels.
  • Fergus County, MT is rural, and covered by Montana's free statewide cadastral program.
  • Gordon County, GA has no open parcel portal. The county sends people to a view-only qPublic site, whose terms forbid scraping, and sells its GIS file at $300 a layer. Georgia has no statewide parcel layer.
inventory/county_sources.csv lists the public endpoint for each layer, found by hand and checked with curl. We count each one live. "Latest date" is the newest date in the layer's date field. That's the best freshness signal these services give, because none of them report an edit date.

Its address theme merges county and state address points, including the USDOT National Address Database. We count the features inside each county outline, split by the dataset each came from. This reads Overture's GeoParquet on S3 with DuckDB, a few minutes per county, and caches the counts in data/.

data.text/markdown: 5. What it adds up to

The catalog. Of Regrid's 40 layers, 12 are public and easy, 17 are public but scattered and 11 are proprietary. The scattered ones are the county record itself: boundaries, owners, values, sales, land use, building attributes. They are public, but only county by county. The proprietary ones are bought from partners (ATTOM deeds, Zoneomics zoning, EarthDefine buildings, Ageon addresses, USPS validation, Esri demographics, NatureServe) or are Regrid's own keys and crosswalks. Of Mireye's 538 fields, 358 come from public national datasets, 15 clip public layers to a parcel, and 165 are licensed parcel fields. 161 of those 165 parcel fields carry Regrid's column names. Regrid's freshness. 87.6% of counties and 92.3% of parcels were refreshed in the last year, against a 92% county target and a 94% parcel claim. 121 counties are over two years old. Some advertised fields are close to empty: tax amount is 14% filled nationwide and 0% in 2697 counties; FEMA flood zone is 0% in 758 counties, though the layer is free. The counties. Wake County publishes everything Regrid sells there except the licensed add-ons, and its own parcel layer was updated more recently than Regrid's copy. Fergus County's parcels and addresses are public through Montana, but we found no machine-readable zoning; Regrid reports 2,937 parcels in a standardized zone there. Montana's parcels carry a property type on 99% of parcels, where Regrid's land use code is 0% filled. Gordon County has no open parcels or addresses: Regrid has 28,899 parcels with owners and values there, bought from a county that sells them, and 31,415 addresses. Open buildings (Overture) reach 88%, 72%, 78% of Regrid's licensed building counts in the three counties. The FEMA maps are old in two of the three: the latest FIRM panel dates are Wake NC 2022-07-19, Fergus MT 2010-07-22, Gordon GA 2008-09-26.

What this doesn't show, and what didn't work

  • Ratings are judgement. The line between "public and easy" and "scattered" is how much work it takes, and each row says why. A statewide parcel program (North Carolina, Montana) turns a scattered layer into an easy one for that state only.
  • Three counties are three examples, not a sample. The national figures come from Regrid's own report.
  • Counts aren't quality. We didn't check that a public parcel matches Regrid's boundary or that a value is the same. Regrid's fill rates and ours count slightly different things ("filled" vs "valid").
  • Freshness is a proxy. No service reports an edit date, so we use the newest date field (sale date, update date). Montana's cadastral has no date field at all; its metadata says it's published monthly.
  • What failed. Some ArcGIS servers treat an empty string as NULL, so field <> '' matched nothing and our first run showed Wake's own parcels with 0% owners; CHAR_LENGTH(field) > 0 works everywhere. api.census.gov now needs a key, so housing units come from TIGERweb. The National Address Database times out on any attribute filter, so we query it by bounding box, which also counts neighbours. Wake's own address service has no date field. Old Montana gisservicemt.gov URLs return an HTML "moved" page.
  • Not tested: Mireye's values. Its Fetch call needs a key from a sign-up, so we rated its catalog without calling it. Regrid's sample files are behind a store page; we used only its public coverage report.
  • The Gordon County parcel layer on a City of Calhoun utility server is public but unlicensed and has geometry and street names only. We count it as a finding, not as a source.
